lr41.argument: A reader might point to 'on a bad month it is forty books and a rainy lunch period' as evidence of dwindling supply, but the passage never suggests the swap is threatened; the writer expects 'the habit... will outlast whichever way the vote goes.' The key's 'fifth anniversary' framing is also a slight inference: 'five Octobers ago' dates the swap but the passage does not present itself as an anniversary piece. Still, the pending vote ('whichever way the vote goes,' 'restore the budget tomorrow') is clearly the occasion.
lr41.stem_issue: The 'fifth anniversary' element of the key is inferred from 'five Octobers ago' rather than stated; the passage never frames itself as an anniversary reflection, though no alternative is better.

lr41.argument: The writer addresses the budget and vote so directly ('I would rather the board restore the budget tomorrow') that a reader might assume the board is the audience. But the board is consistently referred to in the third person ('anyone who tells the school board otherwise is handing them an excuse'), and the writer never says 'you' to board members, so the audience is those around the board rather than the board itself.

The paragraph does claim 'The ledger has taught me more about the reading life of this town than any survey could,' and devotes several clauses to what the ledger reveals. But the option's 'district's own surveys' is not in the passage, and the ledger is one of several examples of 'handling,' which the paragraph explicitly names as 'the answer' to its opening question.

The writer does say 'I would rather the board restore the budget tomorrow' and 'The budget may come back; I hope it does,' so a reader might center the thesis on restoration. But the passage explicitly says the habit 'will outlast whichever way the vote goes' and that the swap 'does' something the library 'never quite did,' so lasting accomplishment is not conditioned on restoration.

The sentence sits right after mention that Mrs. Avendale 'went from full time to two days a week,' so a careless reader might attach it to the staffing cut. But the sentence is about dollars and hardcovers, and the following sentences ('they simply stopped growing,' 'not in the catalog') concern the collection, not staffing.

One could read 'I would rather the board restore the budget' as softening the preceding warning, but it actually reinforces it: having said that overselling the swap 'is handing them an excuse,' the writer shows he would gladly be 'put... out of business.' No contrast with the previous admissions.
lr41.stem_issue: The stem refers to 'his own warning,' but the passage never identifies the writer's gender; the pronoun imports an assumption not supported by the text.

lr41.argument: Both sides of the colon are grammatically independent clauses ('There is one thing the swap does...' / 'it makes children into givers of books'), so a reader might call them two independent observations. But the second clause names the 'one thing' the first merely announces; they are not 'equally important' parallel observations but setup and payoff.

The phrase does echo paragraph 1's 'two folding tables,' so a reader might see a callback. But the echo shows the swap has remained small ('I do not want to make the swap sound larger than it is'), not that it 'has expanded'; the option's purpose is contradicted by the sentence it follows.

lr42.argument: A reader might argue the sentence partly reopens the question raised in ¶3 ("unless we have quietly decided that deserving means being known") by conceding the givers' goodness. But the sentence does not concede that Lenore's page was 'more deserving'; the writer has flatly said Aurelio 'was not less deserving.' The sentence is about the donors' conduct ('Nobody who gave did anything wrong'), which exactly matches the key's framing of forestalling an accusation against donors, and ¶6's 'you who gave twenty dollars or two hundred' confirms donors are the addressed audience.

One could note that pairing 'twenty dollars' with 'two hundred' acknowledges differences in amount, and ¶2 mentions donations with notes. But nothing ranks the gifts; the point of the address is that the instruction to 'Remember' applies to all givers, and ¶4 says they 'did, in fact, something lovely' regardless of sum. The key is clearly correct.

The sentence immediately before the niece's report says 'the money was real,' and a reader might link the detail to the campaign's material success listed in ¶2 (dialysis share, gas, rent). But the detail about opening the page 'before the pill organizer, before the coffee' is about emotional reliance, illustrating 'and so was the comfort,' not the financial coverage, which is narrated in ¶2 rather than ¶4.

A partial reader could say the sentence grants that the system did work for a well-known person ('It worked for her... because she was a story that was easy to tell'), seemingly conceding the arrangement functions for those 'widely known.' But 'for a while' and 'even that was not enough in the end' directly deny reliability, and the writer never withdraws 'It does not work'; the concession is bounded. Option 2's 'reliably' and 'withdrawing the denial' overstate the text.

The clause 'I am not sure the two can be done in the same breath' could be read as hinting that honesty will crowd out honoring. But the column plainly does honor Lenore (¶2's portrait, ¶6's 'Remember the mittens, the snow, the grin'), so the writer does not 'decline to honor the figure at all.' The key correctly identifies the two-part movement, with ¶3's 'Here is the part the eulogies have skipped' as the hinge. Minor quibble: ¶6 interweaves both tasks rather than keeping them strictly sequential, but the key's 'first... afterward' is still a fair description of the overall order.

Since ¶3 challenges the community ('unless we have quietly decided that deserving means being known, being photographed well'), a careless reader might see the opening as undercutting the earlier praise. But the writer never calls that praise insincere; ¶4 explicitly affirms 'they did, in fact, something lovely' and ¶6 tells readers to 'Remember the mittens.' The sentence announces omitted material and a turn, exactly as the key says.

Strictly counted, the second clause ('what no person should have to ask for') is one word longer than the first ('what one person chooses to give'), so a reader fixating on length could pick option 0. But the difference is not 'noticeably' longer, and nothing in the passage frames justice as 'more complicated and contested'; the writer's next sentence relies on the contrast between voluntary giving and what 'no person should have to ask for,' which the parallel frame foregrounds. The key's explanation accurately quotes the differing words.

lw41.argument: Option [1] ("can be installed in about an afternoon by any member who owns a sturdy ladder") is the only other choice addressed to members as doers and gestures at a do-it-yourself, hands-on ethic that gardeners might hold. But it is a logistics sentence, not a reminder of shared values, and does not 'end the flyer' with an appeal. Option [0] is a threat, [2] is a national generalization. The key's link to sharing "extra seedlings and spare tools with neighbors" squarely matches the stated goal.

Option [1] ("The garden should buy a signal booster for the shed roof so that its Wi-Fi reaches farther into the gravel lot") is a genuinely arguable claim that previews the proposal in sentence 9, and it uses the passage's own phrasing ("signal booster mounted on the shed roof"). However, it previews only the booster, omits the table (sentence 10), and does not preview the response to members' concerns (sentences 12-13), so it fails two of the three stated criteria. Options [0] and [3] are factual background, not arguable theses.
lw41.key_flaw: The key's phrase "without harming a single plot" previews only the trampling worry, not the trash worry in sentence 12; and "warm" slightly overstates the passage, which only promises "somewhere other than a cold car" under an outdoor awning. Minor, but the justification claims it 'answers the worry' when it answers half of it.
lw41.stem_issue: Sentence 3 sits at the end of the opening paragraph before the writer introduces herself in sentence 4; a thesis that mentions the 140-dollar cost and plots before any of that is set up is slightly awkward, but the stem's criteria are clear and specific.

lw41.argument: Option [1] ("the hotspot still drops out when it rains on the ridge") does continue the theme of unreliable access and shows the problem persists even after a plan change, which loosely supports the need for a reliable connection. But it does not explain how Caleb's failed quiz itself supports the claim; it adds a new detail rather than interpreting the anecdote. Key [2] explicitly draws the inference ("the connection decided his grade more than his effort did").

Option [1] is the most concise of the four and opens with the hours information ("Because the garden already stays open until dusk"), so a reader might argue it retains the idea that no hours change is needed. But "at all hours" contradicts the passage (the garden closes at dusk) and the sentence never states that no new hours would be needed; it also drops "with one outdoor outlet" placement detail less cleanly. Option [2]'s "although... anyway" creates an illogical contrast; option [3] is a comma splice ending in a fragment ("so no new hours").
lw41.key_flaw: The key is not notably more concise than the two original sentences combined (it is roughly the same length or slightly longer), so the stem's 'concisely' is satisfied only relative to the other options; the justification's claim of concision is mild overstatement.

lw42.argument: No non-key option has a case. [0] contradicts sentence 11 outright ("no student will ever repeat a class again"). [2] describes advisors' demeanor, not lost time. [3] supports sentence 9's tuition point ("because tuition is lower"), not the retaking-courses claim. Only [1] supplies a concrete instance of "repeated three passed courses, costing her a full extra semester," which directly matches sentence 11's "lose a semester or more retaking classes he or she has already passed."

[0] does satisfy the first half of the stated goal—it concedes that "so many courses fall outside these agreements"—so a partial reader attending only to the 'admits limits' clause might select it. But it fails the second half: recommending that students be "better off skipping community college entirely" undercuts the post's purpose ("Hope to see you there") rather than arguing for attendance. [2] overclaims ("every class... any degree at any university") and admits no limit; [1] is irrelevant decor. [3] alone concedes the limit and converts it into a reason to attend ("which is exactly why a conversation with an advisor... is worth an evening").

lr21.argument: Paragraph 4 opens 'We have seen this before, two miles away' and devotes a whole paragraph to Marrow Lane's collapse ('a third of the chosen vendors had given up their leases'), so a reader skimming for the most vivid event might take that failure as the occasion. But the passage never says the city is 'reconsidering' pavilions because of it; Marrow Lane is evidence, not occasion. The occasion is unambiguous: 'the Orrisport Redevelopment Council has published its plan' and 'you have until the end of the month to amend this plan.'

The writer does accept a roof: 'You can give Halvern Street a roof,' and she concedes 'The wiring on Halvern Street is a genuine hazard.' A partial reader could call this 'reluctant endorsement of the pavilion.' But she explicitly rejects the pavilion's defining features ('sixty identical stalls, a central payment kiosk,' selection, lottery, rents) and demands 'leave the stalls where they are,' so 'regret that the old stalls will be lost' misstates her position—she argues they need not be lost.

Paragraph 2 celebrates that the market 'accumulated' and the city 'for sixty years mostly left it alone,' which could suggest the thesis is simple non-intervention. However paragraph 6 flatly contradicts 'entirely alone': 'None of this means the market should stay dangerous. Fix the wiring... Lay proper drains.' The key accurately combines the definition of character (¶5) with the prescription (¶6).

The franchise-and-candles detail follows directly from 'a third of the chosen vendors had given up their leases,' and paragraph 3 flags rents 'substantially above current informal levels' as an objection, so a reader might link the vacancies to rent and read the detail as supporting [3]. But the passage never states why Marrow Lane vendors left, and 'within a single season' is not in the text; the detail itself is about what the committee installed, i.e., the outcome of selection, matching the key.

Paragraph 5 does grant that the renderings 'reproduce so lovingly' the lanterns, sailcloth, and signs, which resembles a concession about the renderings' accuracy. But the paragraph then argues that look is not character ('You cannot photograph the tolerance') and never turns to cost; cost appears only in paragraph 3. The key's 'redefines the key term' is well supported by 'But character, in a market, is not a look. It is a set of habits...'

'so lovingly' carries a faint irony—the Council lavishes affection on surfaces while planning to remove the people—so one could read it as gentle mockery of planners' sentimentality. But [2] adds that the writer 'refuses to indulge' sentimentality, which the passage contradicts: she opens with 'forty small flames in a row like a procession that had decided to stand still' and closes on 'someone who knows where the lanterns are.' And 'I want to be fair to the people who wrote it' rules out mockery as the primary function; the key's 'sincere but aimed at the wrong thing' fits 'But character, in a market, is not a look.'

A reader might infer causation—the pavilion's construction (via lottery) disperses the habits—and treat the semicolon as 'therefore.' But the two clauses are parallel measurements of time ('eighteen months' vs. 'sixty years'), not cause and effect; the destruction of habits is attributed to the lottery in the third clause, not to construction. [2] is grammatically wrong (a semicolon coordinates, not subordinates), and [0] is wrong because no list follows.

The sentence is dated to 1987 and told about 'my aunt,' and the writer elsewhere says vendors asked for wiring 'since before I was born,' so one could argue the dated opening marks a secondhand memory. But nothing in the arrangement signals distance—the writer says 'I think of those lanterns now' as if remembered—and the question asks what the fronted clause emphasizes, which is clearly the main-clause verb 'kept frying' set against the power failure. [3] fails because the blackout is not presented as a hazard, and [2] because no decline is described.

lr24.argument: A reader might infer from 'a parent watching a child's enthusiasm curdle at the first hard page' that the writer has observed children learning, and the school is called a 'Community Music School,' so children could plausibly be enrolled. But the passage never says the writer teaches children; the writer says 'I have taught cello at the school for eleven years' and speaks only of 'adult students,' so [0] asserts something unsupported. The key's reading—that the sentence addresses 'you,' whether 'an adult thinking about picking up an instrument, or a parent,' and asks both to 'notice which kind of failure is on offer in the room'—is clearly what the clause does.

A careless reader might take '22 of 26 still enrolled' as evidence the dropout problem is fixed. But the passage explicitly contrasts the Wednesday group 'against a school-wide retention rate of roughly half,' and ¶1 reports the recital was still canceled this March, so the school-wide problem is not resolved; the figures are local to the Wednesday group. [2] is directly contradicted by 'They do not play better than the others, at least not at first.' Key is sound.

The tag 'whatever talent is' does express skepticism about the concept of talent, and a reader could take it as dismissive. But the sentence's main clause concedes a limit ('is not the same thing as talent'), follows 'I do not want to overstate what a Wednesday can do,' and never claims the method is 'the only real factor'; the writer elsewhere says students 'do not play better.' So [2] inverts the sentence's qualifying function. [3] has no support: the writer never allows that the verdict can be accurate.
lr24.stem_issue: Option [2]'s 'whatever talent is' hook is a slight distractor; otherwise fine.

lr24.argument: Paragraph 2 does display the teacher's close observation ('she taped her fingerboard, counted aloud, and arrived early to tune'), which contributes to credibility. But credibility is established chiefly in ¶1 ('I have taught cello at the school for eleven years'), and ¶3 recommends no exercise—the exercise appears in ¶5. [3] is contradicted by ¶1's 'I have watched this happen every spring,' which marks Ruth as typical, not unusual. The key is clearly supported by ¶3's opening 'That distinction is the one I most want adult learners to understand.'
lr24.key_flaw: The justification refers to 'sentence 11,' a numbering not visible to the test-taker (it does correspond to the last sentence of ¶2 if counted from the passage start, but the reference is opaque).

lr24.argument: The mechanic image does convey matter-of-fact seriousness, and the next sentence raises the 'faintly ridiculous' point, so one could argue the simile pre-empts that charge. But the writer immediately concedes the exercise 'is faintly ridiculous, and the students know it,' so the comparison is not deployed to counter that sense. Its function is to depict adults treating error as 'a report about what your hand did'—'the thumb got left behind' said 'with the calm of mechanics'—exactly the information stance from ¶3. [2] and [3] misread 'calm' as indifference or reduce cello to mechanics, which the passage does not do.

No alternative has a case. [0] fails because the 'not... ; they are...' structure rejects one description, not balances two. [1] fails because the second clause gives a positive definition ('they are people who have learned to hear a wrong note as a question'). [3] contradicts the sentence, which says professionals have not 'stopped making mistakes.'

One could read 'They quit less' as letting results speak for themselves after the writer called the exercise 'faintly ridiculous.' But the writer agrees the exercise is ridiculous ('and the students know it') and does not dismiss the view; the short sentence instead narrows the claim after conceding 'They do not play better than the others.' [3] misreads modesty as frustration; [0] has no basis—the writer never urges adoption everywhere and in fact says 'I do not want to overstate what a Wednesday can do.'
lr24.stem_issue: The stem says the sentence follows 'the longer sentences about retention figures,' but the immediately preceding sentence is 'They do not play better than the others, at least not at first,' which is about skill, not retention. Minor inaccuracy; the key's justification correctly notes the 'do not play better' disclaimer.

lr24.argument: A reader might see the colon list as the hinge of the paragraph, since the direct address to the reader comes soon after. But the turn to the reader occurs two sentences later with 'But if you are an adult thinking about picking up an instrument,' and the colon itself sits inside the concession, not at its boundary. [2] fails since no ranking of reasons is implied; [3] fails because the reasons are the students', and the writer never discusses leaving teaching. The key correctly identifies that the particulars ('a grandchild who needs the spare room where the cello lived') give the general concession humane weight.

lw43.argument: Option [3] is the only alternative that preserves the exact wording of the original sentence 3 ('She is the only person on the stage who makes no sound') and adds factual context, so a reader who thinks 'revise' means 'minimally extend' might pick it. But it poses no puzzle at all; 'she has led the orchestra for many seasons' does not ask how silent leadership works, which the stem explicitly requires. Option [1] raises a question, but the wrong one (selection of conductors, never addressed in paragraphs 2–3). Option [2] asserts a conclusion ('proves') rather than posing an investigation, and the paragraphs that follow do not argue importance. The key is the only option that both keeps the silent-player fact and frames the investigative question that sentences 4–10 then answer.
lw43.stem_issue: The stem nearly dictates the answer by restating the puzzle ('how a person who makes no sound can still lead the players'), which makes the item easy, but the goal is narrow and clear, so this is a difficulty issue rather than a defect.

lw43.argument: Option [1] mentions 'breathing exercises,' so a careless reader keyed on the word 'breath' in sentence 4 might select it. However, it concerns wind players' own breathing for sustaining notes, not the orchestra following the conductor's breath 'more closely than her baton,' so it offers no evidence for the cellist's specific comparative claim. Option [0] actually contradicts the claim (eyes 'fixed on the tip of the conductor's baton'). Option [3] is irrelevant to breath or baton. The key's 'rising shoulders, not the baton tip' is the only option that supplies a second witness to the breath-over-baton point and mirrors the comparative structure of sentence 4.

Option [3], 'Like a traffic officer at a busy corner, she stood in the center where everyone could see her,' is the only alternative whose vehicle (a traffic officer) is itself someone whose hand gestures are conventional signals that drivers have learned to read, so it loosely gestures toward the argument. But the sentence's actual point of comparison is visibility and position ('stood in the center where everyone could see her'), not learned meaning; it says nothing about the lowered hand meaning 'softer' or about the players having learned the code. Option [1] is purely descriptive imagery of the fading sound and advances no argument; option [2] ('create the music entirely by herself') actually undercuts the argument that players read and respond to her signals, and sits awkwardly after a paragraph about the brass responding. The key alone makes the learned-shared-meaning point explicit ('meant softer only because the players had learned it together') and ties directly to the hand gesture in sentence 10.

lw44.argument: Option [2] ("Public pools across the country offer recreation, safety training, and relief from summer heat") is the only distractor that is at least a reasonable, well-written topic-level claim about pools, and it generalizes sentence 2's "Pools are important to communities in many ways." But it is impersonal and generic, says nothing about what the pool "came to mean to her," and does not preview the essay's actual thread ("The pool brings together people who would never otherwise meet"). Option [0] is personal but slangy and empty; [1] is a factual aside. The key, "strangers become neighbors," ties directly to sentences 5 and 6.

Option [3] ("The evening lifeguards were reassigned to the morning shift, which was already fully staffed") does describe a consequence of the cut and could be read as showing the decision was wasteful, but it addresses staffing, not "the role she says the pool plays in the community" (bringing together "people who would never otherwise meet"). The key explicitly connects the lost hours to "the only time many working parents could bring their children" (sentence 10) and to the neighbor-making role. Option [1] contradicts the essay's point; [0] is irrelevant.

Option [2] ("reports the water temperature, which is recorded hourly on a clipboard") is the only distractor that avoids hostility, but it is flatly informational and strips out the gentle humor entirely, so it fails the stated goal of keeping an "affectionate, gently amused tone." Options [1] and [3] ("rudely," "annoyingly lectures," "like I am clueless") are openly irritated. The original's "as if I had not measured it myself" is the only wording that conveys fond amusement.
lw44.stem_issue: The stem refers to an "underlined portion" but the text is merely quoted, not underlined; cosmetic only.

lw44.argument: Option [1] ("I learned that a public space stays public, so its users show up wherever decisions are made") is just as concise as the key and removes the repetition, but "so" reverses the logic of sentence 12 ("only stays public if the people who use it are willing to show up and speak up"), turning a condition into a result. Option [0] is concise but drops the lesson's specific content; [2] keeps the repetition. The key preserves the conditional "only if" and both "show up and speak up."

Option [0] ("open, so it cut") is grammatically a correct joining of two independent clauses with a comma and coordinating conjunction, but "so" expresses result rather than the required contrast between keeping the pool open and cutting hours. Option [1] misplaces the comma after "but"; option [3] is a comma splice. Only the original "open, but it cut" satisfies both the grammar and the contrast requirement.
lw44.stem_issue: The keyed option [2] is word-for-word the existing text but is not labeled "(as it is now)," and the stem's wording ("join the two independent clauses correctly") implies the current sentence is flawed when it is not; a careful student may hesitate to select an unmarked no-change option. Minor.

sw45.argument: Option [3] ("The Tamsett Trail Association has kept the path open for many years, and its crews have rebuilt dozens of washed-out sections") could be read as indirectly reassuring: an experienced organization implies competent supervision, and it ties back to sentence 9's "wash out the drainage ditches." But it never addresses inexperience directly and contains no call to join, so it fails the second half of the stated goal. Options [1] and [2] actively work against the goal: [1] tells readers that "only students in excellent physical shape should think about signing up," heightening rather than easing worry, and [2] addresses "Experienced hikers who already know how to swing a pulaski," excluding the target audience. The key explicitly states "No experience is needed," explains why ("crew leaders teach every task on the spot"), and ends with "come help keep the trail open."
sw45.stem_issue: Minor: the stem refers to "classmates," but the passage itself never identifies the audience as students or a school; the reader must accept this framing from the stem alone. It does not affect the answer.

sw45.argument: Option [2] ("As a result of this slow building process, maintenance never ends") does bridge paragraph 2's topic ("Building a trail is slower than most people imagine") to the maintenance paragraph and keeps the original clause "maintenance never ends." However, it asserts a cause-effect relationship the passage never supports: maintenance is needed because "storms knock trees across the path and wash out the drainage ditches" (sentence 9), not because building was slow. The key, "Yet finishing a stretch of trail is only the beginning, because maintenance never ends," correctly signals a contrast/continuation and makes explicit that work continues after construction, matching the stem. Options [0] ("Similarly... never ends either") and [1] ("For instance") use transitions that misrepresent the logical relationship, and [1] invents a detail about Bramble Gap not in the passage.
